title: White House Says Local Communities Should Decide Future of Texas Data Center Approvals
summary:
The White House said that decisions on the approval and placement of new data centers in Texas should be left to local residents. The response follows a pledge by Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa to freeze new construction permits for the industry until the state enacts laws to protect water availability and prevent electricity price increases for rural consumers.

The proposed moratorium will not affect projects that have already secured permits, which Hinojosa said covers most facilities scheduled for delivery through 2028. The freeze would remain in effect until the state legislature passes new protections, potentially during the next session that runs for 140 days between January and May 2027.

The governor-elect of Texas, Gina Hinojosa, has explicitly said that all currently permitted datacenters in Texas will be allowed to finish construction. This essentially covers all of the 2027 and likely well into 2028.

She is going to pass laws that ensure that all *newly* permitted datacenters going forward for delivery in 2028/2029 will pay taxes, commit to no increase in power prices for consumers, don’t impact water availability for people, be constructed with union labor and give “Texans a seat at the table.”

Sounds reasonable. She doesn’t want to lose a lot of good blue collar jobs and property taxes for small towns in rural Texas.

Datacenter commentary starts at 6:30 in this interview.

Also attaching her official campaign position from her website in the next post.

Sidenote: After watching a bunch of her speeches and interviews, I do think she is a political talent and probably has a future in national politics.

selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa: “It is not that I hate data centers. I hate the way they are taking advantage of Texas”

Asked whether data centers still have a future in Texas:

HINOJOSA: “Right. Well, we have always been a pro-business state in Texas. But what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans. And right now what has happened is data centers have moved into mostly rural communities and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans and Texans are being taken advantage of. So the difference is we will have laws to protect Texans and we need to stop what we’re doing with data centers until we have those protections. We can have a strong economy, strong industry and protections for the people of Texas. Those things are not mutually exclusive, and I’ll make sure as governor I lead to ensure that that happens.”

TAPPER: “So you’re not ruling out that data centers will be able to be built in Texas, it’s just you want there to be regulations to protect communities, is that right?”

HINOJOSA: “And that communities have a seat at the table to decide if and how these data centers come into their communities. Texas is like a country. We are so diverse in all the ways. Different communities have different needs. And those communities have to be able to walk away from the table to leverage what they need for their community. So absolutely, we need to make sure they are partners in this effort. And that has always been my position. It is not that I hate data centers. I hate the way they are taking advantage of Texas. And that stops when I’m governor.”

selectedTweets.text:
@GavinSBaker Great post, and here are a few additional points around the margins:

- She indeed says that there will be a moratorium ON APPROVALS until a new law is passed that gives Texans a seat at the table.  Yes, this does mean that previously approved data centers can continue construction.

- On the new law being passed: Texas has an odd legislative calendar, in which legislative sessions run for 140 days *every 2 years*.  The next one runs between January and May 2027.  If the law that Hinojosa is talking about fails to be enacted as a result of this legislative session, the next one doesn't start until January 2029.

The bad news is that this is a very short time window, which means that interested parties need to start working with legislature members on this bill NOW.  I hope the industry's government relations teams are already on it.

The good news is that, if the bill is successfully passed, the moratorium won't be long at all - probably one year at most (and could even be significantly shorter).

selectedTweets.text:
I understand that beating up on data centers is politically popular. But what problem are we actually solving?

The Community Note helps, but “new permits/approvals” still leaves a lot unanswered. What happens to projects already in the pipeline that need another approval? The devil’s in the details. Let’s see what she actually proposes.

We were involved in the Brazos bankruptcy. I have no illusions about how messy the Texas power market can get. But interruptible demand has value: crypto miners can curtail, and suitably designed data centers can shift or reduce certain workloads when the grid is stressed. Build that flexibility into the deal.

Make developers pay for the infrastructure they require. Address water use based on the actual cooling system and local supply. Require enforceable curtailment commitments where feasible.

That sounds like policy. “Halt data centers” sounds like political grandstanding.

Speaking as a distressed investor: bring on the volatility. More opportunity for us. Still a lousy way to encourage investment.
